summary: The specification of Datalanguage version 0/9, the language of the Datacomputer, a data storage and management utility being developed for the ARPANET. This early version is described as extremely primitive, with elementary items limited to fixed-length ASCII strings. Later versions were planned to remove that restriction.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC specifies Datalanguage version 0/9, used with the Datacomputer for storing and managing data. It defines data structures and requests for creating, transferring, and selecting data.

subtitle: The syntax and operations of the Datacomputer's Datalanguage version 0/9.

tldr.problem: The Datacomputer needed a language for describing stored data and requesting storage, retrieval, and other data operations.
tldr.mechanism: Datalanguage 0/9 describes hierarchical containers and provides commands to create, open, close, transfer, select, and delete data.
tldr.outcome: The RFC specifies an early version that the preface calls extremely primitive, with elementary items restricted to fixed-length ASCII strings.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 515's status as Unknown. The RFC describes version 0/9 and says later versions were planned to offer greater Datalanguage capabilities.

sections.title: Datalanguage and the Datacomputer
sections.content:
Datalanguage is the language processed by the Datacomputer, a data storage and management utility being developed for the ARPANET. The RFC specifies version 0/9, which the preface says was running at CCA and was extremely primitive.

The RFC organizes its specification around data description, a directory, data-management operations, name recognition, and syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: Datalanguage lets a user describe data and ask the Datacomputer to manage it. This RFC documents version 0/9, an early and limited version.

sections.title: Containers and Data Structure
sections.content:
Datalanguage describes data as containers. The three types are LIST, which holds repeated containers of the same description; STRUCT, which holds described components; and STRING, a sequence of ASCII characters.

Containers can be nested. A directory stores names and descriptions, and a pathname identifies a node by joining the names along its path.
sections.plainLanguage: A LIST holds repeated items, a STRUCT groups named parts, and a STRING holds text. These containers can be nested to describe data.

sections.title: Managing and Moving Data
sections.content:
Requests include CREATE, DELETE, OPEN, CLOSE, MODE, CONNECT, DISCONNECT, and LIST. Open containers can be in READ, WRITE, or APPEND mode, and assignment transfers data from one container to another.

FOR applies operations to members of a list and can select a subset by content. Ports associate containers with external addresses for data transmission; CONNECT and DISCONNECT change those associations.
sections.plainLanguage: Users can create and open containers, transfer data between them, and select list members by their contents. Ports connect data containers to external addresses.

sections.title: Version 0/9 Restrictions
sections.content:
In version 0/9, elementary data items are fixed-length ASCII strings, and files are a restricted class of hierarchical structures. The RFC marks some restrictions with three asterisks and says they refer to limits expected to be weakened or removed in the next software version.

The document also specifies how requests are parsed, including separators, comments, reserved identifiers, and the BNF syntax.
sections.plainLanguage: Version 0/9 has restrictions, including fixed-length ASCII strings. The RFC identifies some limits as ones the next software version was expected to change.
